claims.text: In its author's disclosure, Searchbloom says it publishes the list and ranks itself first.
The publisher says its facts come from company websites and its case-study figures are the companies' own reporting.
The publisher recommends defining success as leads, sign-ups, or revenue from AI referrals, rather than citation counts or visibility scores.
It recommends requesting a dated AI search result with a named or described company, a figure, and a period.
AI answers are probabilistic: repeating the same question can produce different brands.
The publisher recommends tracking a fixed set of real buyer questions daily across the AI platforms buyers use, then reading the trend.
It recommends separating branded from non-branded prompts and segmenting them by awareness, consideration, and purchase.
Its suggested metrics are visibility, share of voice, average position, win rate, and sentiment.
Buyers should ask which tracking tool, prompts, platforms, and run frequency an agency uses.
In Searchbloom's own tracking, about nine of every ten sources AI cites are on other people's sites.
Buyers should request the outside URLs retrieved and cited for their top buyer questions, including which placements the agency can help secure.
When an answer omits a business, the publisher recommends inspecting its cited pages; often, the fix is a listing through outreach, a review, or sponsorship.
Crawler access, correct structured data, and clean architecture make a site legible to AI platforms.
The agency should run on-site technical, content, and entity work.
The agency should establish AI visibility tracking and review it with the client monthly.

The client's team must own sponsorship and affiliate budgets when the most-retrieved roundup in its category is a paid placement; it must also own retailer, marketplace, and partner listings, social media and community work, and brand positioning and the budget behind PR.
Buyers should clarify whether the agency builds technical changes or supplies recommendations, and price the developer time they must provide.
Of the nine listed companies, three publish a fee, two a minimum, and four a contract term.
The publisher recommends obtaining unpublished fees, minimums, and contract lengths in writing before comparing agencies.
The publisher flags promises of AI citations in weeks and reports that count citations without mentioning leads or revenue.
